Mathematical logic

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Foundations of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 25k Articles: 518
Mathematical logic studies formal languages, formal proofs, model theory, computability theory, and the foundations of mathematics. It makes the rules of reasoning explicit enough that reasoning itself becomes an object of mathematics. Proof theory studies deductions; model theory studies interpretations in which statements hold.
Three questions organize the subject: is an expression a well-formed first-order formula, is it true in a specified first-order structure, and does it have a formal proof from specified axioms? These questions are distinct. For example, ∃n(n+n=1) is a first-order sentence in an appropriate first-order language; it is false in the natural numbers but true in the rational numbers, with n=1/2.
The beauty of mathematical logic is that the same logical connectives and rules of universal quantification and existential quantification organize arguments across mathematics. Classical propositional logic uses two truth values; Intuitionistic propositional logic interprets logical implication through constructions on proofs, without unrestricted law of excluded middle. This proof-based framework is developed in Frank Pfenning, Natural Deduction, sections 1–3.

Logical formula (ϕ)

Words: 93 Articles: 1
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
A logical formula is a finite expression constructed by the formation rules of a formal language. Propositional formulas combine propositional variables by logical connectives. First-order formulas additionally contain terms, atomic relations and quantifiers. A logical formula is a syntactic object; its truth is determined only after specifying a suitable interpretation and values for its free variables.

Logical variable (x)

Words: 47
Logical formula OurBigBook.com
A logical variable is a symbol whose value is supplied by the semantics of a logical language. A propositional variable receives a truth value under a Boolean valuation. An individual variable of first-order logic receives an element of a structure under an assignment. These are different kinds of variable and should not be identified.

Logical fixed point

Words: 74
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
A logical fixed point is a formula or sentence equivalent to the result of applying a specified formula operation to itself. In arithmetic, self-reference is mediated by a Gödel number and the diagonal lemma, yielding a first-order sentence G with a provable equivalence G↔H(┌G┐). In modal logic, a modal formula A satisfies A↔F(A) modulo the chosen logic. A merely true semantic equivalence is weaker than a specified provable or canonical construction, so its hypotheses must be kept distinct.

Second-order logic extends first-order logic by allowing existential quantification and universal quantification over second-order relation variables, as well as over individual objects. In the relational presentation used here, an individual variable x ranges over a domain D, while a second-order relation variable R of arity k denotes a subset of Dk. Unary second-order relation variables denote subsets of D; binary ones denote binary relations. Presentations with function variables can instead describe their graphs by second-order relation variables, with first-order formulas requiring a unique output for every input.
For a graph with vertices D and fixed graph adjacency E, the first-order sentence ∀x∃yE(x,y) says that every vertex has a neighbour. It selects individual vertices while E retains its given interpretation. By contrast,
∃P(∃xP(x) ∧ ∀x∀y((P(x)∧P(y))→¬E(x,y)))
(2)
selects an entire subset P and says that it is a nonempty independent set. Here P is a unary second-order relation variable, rather than a symbol in the input first-order signature. This particular property also has a simple first-order sentence on simple graphs; the example illustrates the change in what can be selected, rather than proving a separation in expressive power.
The usefulness of second-order logic is that one can describe a whole proposed solution, such as a graph coloring, and then impose local constraints on it. Syntax alone does not specify which proposed relations are available: full semantics for second-order logic permits all external subsets of Dk, whereas Henkin semantics supplies designated ranges. The second-order encoding of three-colorability makes this distinction concrete.

Second-order logic OurBigBook.com
A second-order relation variable of arity k≥1 can be assigned a subset of the k-fold Cartesian product Dk; its application R(x1​,…,xk​) is true exactly when the tuple (x1​,…,xk​) belongs to that subset. Arity is the number of arguments, so a unary second-order relation variable is a predicate on individual objects. For a finite set D of cardinality n, there are nk possible tuples and 2nk possible relations under full semantics for second-order logic. A relation is encoded by nk membership bits once the objects have been numbered; the number of possible witnesses can be exponential even when each witness has a short encoding.

An existential second-order logic sentence has the form
∃R1​⋯∃Rm​φ,
(3)
where each Ri​ is a second-order relation variable of fixed finite arity ki​ and φ is a first-order sentence over the input first-order signature expanded by the Ri​. The first-order sentence may contain both universal quantification and existential quantification over individuals; only the outer quantification over second-order relation variables is required to be existential. Under full semantics for second-order logic, truth means that some expansion by witness relations satisfies φ.
For a fixed existential second-order logic sentence on a domain of cardinality n, the witnesses need ∑i=1m​nki​ membership bits. The arities and the number of witnesses are constants because the sentence is fixed. After guessing those bits, a verifier evaluates the fixed first-order sentence by enumerating assignments to its finitely many individual variables, taking polynomial time. In the second-order encoding of three-colorability, the three witnesses require 3n bits, and the edge constraints can be checked over at most n2 ordered vertex pairs. This is the logical form of the NP principle that a positive answer has a short complexity certificate.
The fixed-sentence qualification matters: it is the input first-order structure that varies, rather than an arbitrarily large formula supplied with each input. Fagin's theorem states the converse as well: every isomorphism-invariant NP property of finite relational first-order structures has such a description. The coloring example uses only unary second-order relation variables; the general theorem allows any fixed finite arities.

One(x)Different(x,y)​:=(C1​(x)∨C2​(x)∨C3​(x))∧¬(C1​(x)∧C2​(x))∧¬(C1​(x)∧C3​(x))∧¬(C2​(x)∧C3​(x)),:=¬(C1​(x)∧C1​(y))∧¬(C2​(x)∧C2​(y))∧¬(C3​(x)∧C3​(y)).​
(4)
Then the existential second-order logic sentence
Φ3​:=∃C1​∃C2​∃C3​(∀xOne(x) ∧ ∀x∀y(E(x,y)→Different(x,y)))
(5)
asserts that every vertex receives exactly one of the three colours and adjacent vertices receive different colours. The first clause gives coverage and pairwise disjointness of the three subsets; the second makes each subset an independent set. Empty colour classes are allowed, so Φ3​ expresses existence of a proper vertex coloring using at most three colours.
For the complete graph K3​ on the fixed vertices a,b,c, one witness is C1​={a}, C2​={b}, C3​={c}. Each vertex satisfies exactly one predicate, and each of the three edges joins different predicates. Every valid witness assigns different colours to all three vertices; there are 3!=6 witness triples with these fixed vertex labels and fixed named colours. We are counting assignments, without identifying them under colour permutations or graph isomorphisms. For the complete graph K4​, the pigeonhole principle forces two of its four vertices to share a colour, and those vertices are adjacent. Thus it has no witness triple. This calculation illustrates a complexity certificate without requiring the reader to reconstruct a machine computation.

Fagin's theorem

Words: 341
Existential second-order logic OurBigBook.com
Fix a finite relational first-order signature τ, and let K be a class of finite nonempty τ-first-order structures closed under isomorphism. Fagin's theorem states that K is definable by one existential second-order logic sentence under full semantics for second-order logic if and only if its language of standard finite encodings belongs to NP. A standard encoding numbers the domain {0,…,n−1} and lists membership bits for each input relation, together with n; take an explicit encoding whose length is at least n. The encoding language contains all numbered copies of members of K, with malformed encodings rejected. The isomorphism condition makes membership a property of the structure rather than an arbitrary choice of labels. Changing between the usual explicit encodings preserves the NP characterization by polynomial time translations.
The forward direction is the witness-and-verifier calculation in existential second-order logic. For the reverse direction, the guiding idea is to encode an accepting nondeterministic computation using second-order relation variables: fixed-length tuples of domain elements index enough time steps and storage positions for a polynomial time computation. A first-order sentence checks the initial input, legal transitions, and acceptance. The number of tuples grows with the input, although the checking sentence stays fixed. No total order must be supplied as part of the input first-order signature: an auxiliary total order can itself be existentially guessed and constrained by a first-order sentence. Isomorphism invariance ensures that a change of this auxiliary numbering does not change membership in K.
The second-order encoding of three-colorability is a small instance of the forward direction. The beauty of Fagin's theorem is the complete correspondence: the computational class NP can be characterized by the shape of a logical description, without mentioning a particular machine in the statement. The scope is finite relational first-order structures and fixed sentences; it is not a claim about deciding arbitrary second-order logic sentences or about arbitrary infinite domains.
Ronald Fagin published the result in Generalized First-Order Spectra and Polynomial-Time Recognizable Sets, SIAM-AMS Proceedings 7 (1974), pp. 43–73, Section 4. The original paper frames the correspondence using classes of finite expansions and their encodings. Fagin's author-maintained publication list explains that the abstract in the available copy was added in 2019; its modern summary should therefore not be mistaken for part of the 1974 printing.

Henkin semantics

Words: 360
Second-order logic OurBigBook.com
In Henkin semantics, a domain D is accompanied by designated ranges Hk​⊆P(Dk) for second-order relation variables of each arity k. A formula ∃Rφ(R) searches only Hk​, and ∀Rφ(R) checks only Hk​. These ranges can be proper subcollections of the external power set. Keeping D and its input relations fixed therefore need not fix the truth of a second-order logic sentence.
As a toy illustration of restricted quantification, take D={a,b} and unary range H1​={∅,D}. The sentence
∀a∃P∀x(P(x)↔x=a)
(6)
is true under full semantics for second-order logic, but false with this selected range, because neither singleton is available. Likewise, on the complete graph K3​, the unary range {∅,D} admits no witness for the second-order encoding of three-colorability, even though a usual proper vertex coloring exists. This toy range illustrates the truth definition only: it fails second-order comprehension for the formula x=a, and is not a model of a system requiring that comprehension instance.
Admissible Henkin semantics for a specified deductive system must satisfy its axioms, including its chosen second-order comprehension requirements or analogous closure conditions for predicate abstraction. Closure is relative to the permitted formulas and parameters, rather than a blanket property of every selected family. In particular, on a finite domain, allowing logical equality, individual parameters, all finite logical disjunctions, and comprehension for those formulas forces every finite-arity relation to be available: enumerate its tuples and disjoin the formulas naming them. Thus a proper restricted finite range cannot satisfy that entire scheme.
Treating each Hk​ as an additional sort, with an application relation between its members and k individuals, translates this relational presentation into first-order logic with several sorts. Include axioms saying that predicates with the same members are equal, together with whatever second-order comprehension the system requires. This makes Henkin semantics useful for bringing first-order logic methods to reasoning about predicates; it does not license conclusions about all external relations.
Leon Henkin's Completeness in the Theory of Types, Journal of Symbolic Logic 15 (1950), pp. 81–91 develops general models and proves completeness for his typed deductive system. Its opening footnote 5 explicitly discusses closure under operations associated with formula formation. Henkin later described the discovery process in his [ref]; that later account is a historical recollection, distinct from the original publication.

Full semantics for second-order logic

Words: 269
Second-order logic OurBigBook.com
Under full semantics for second-order logic, a second-order relation variable of arity k ranges over exactly P(Dk), the external power set of the appropriate Cartesian product. Thus
∃Rφ(R)meanssome S⊆Dk satisfies φ(S),
(7)
and universal quantification over R checks every such subset. Here the power set is taken in the ambient mathematical universe, not merely among relations definable by formulas or represented by objects inside D.
For D={a,b,c}, a unary second-order relation variable has eight possible values, including the three singletons needed by the second-order encoding of three-colorability. The three unary witnesses can range independently over those eight subsets, giving 83=512 candidate triples before the first-order sentence is checked; only six triples pass for the complete graph K3​. For K4​, there are 163=4096 candidate triples and none passes. Distinguishing the range of candidates from the constraints on valid witnesses clarifies both full semantics for second-order logic and the verifier view of NP.
The appeal of full semantics for second-order logic is its literal reading of assertions about every subset or every relation. A first-order structure fixes the second-order ranges automatically, in contrast to Henkin semantics. That expressive force comes with a limitation: there is no effective, sound deductive system complete for all valid second-order logic sentences under full semantics for second-order logic. This limitation and the change of intended models motivating Henkin semantics are described at the start of [ref].
For a domain Vλ​, an external functional graph with all its individual ordered pairs in Vλ​ is therefore available, even if the whole graph does not belong to Vλ​. More generally, a binary second-order relation variable can denote any external subset of Vλ​×Vλ​; its ordered pairs need not themselves be elements of the individual domain. Having endpoints in the domain is what matters. This distinction between internal objects and externally available relations is essential when applying second-order logic to the cumulative hierarchy.

Second-order logic OurBigBook.com
Second-order comprehension is a scheme asserting the existence of a second-order relation variable whose members are exactly the tuples satisfying a permitted formula:
∃R∀x1​⋯∀xk​(R(x1​,…,xk​)↔φ(x1​,…,xk​,aˉ,Sˉ)).
(8)
Here R is not free in φ, and the displayed individual and relation parameters are universally closed in each instance. Under full semantics for second-order logic, the selected external subset of Dk is always available. Under Henkin semantics, the selected subset must lie in Hk​ for every allowed assignment of parameters. Different systems permit different formula classes: for example, arithmetical comprehension theory restricts comprehension to formulas without bound set variables, while still permitting set parameters. Consequently, the exact formula and parameter policy must accompany any claim that a restricted range satisfies second-order comprehension.

The logic Lω1​,ω​ extends first-order logic by countable logical conjunctions and logical disjunctions. Each formula has finitely many free variables, and quantifier strings are finite. Every countable structure in a countable first-order language has a Scott sentence. Hence countable structures satisfying the same sentences of countable infinitary logic are isomorphic. The proof uses Scott formulas, stabilization on the countable set of finite tuples, and the back-and-forth method.

Propositional logic

Words: 7k Articles: 152
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
Propositional logic studies reasoning with whole propositions represented by letters such as p and q, and propositional formulas built from them using logical connectives. The classical two-valued, truth-functional presentation below assigns each primitive proposition either true or false: each compound value depends only on its component values. This is classical propositional logic; other systems, including Intuitionistic propositional logic, have different semantics and rules.
Starting with p and q, one can build ¬p by logical negation, p∧q by logical conjunction, p∨q by logical disjunction, and p→q by logical implication, then combine these into larger propositional formulas. Parentheses specify the construction: (p→q)∧p has logical conjunction as its outermost logical connective. Primitive propositions have no internal structure in this language; a first-order formula can additionally describe objects and quantify over them. The formation rules are given in forall x: Calgary, chapter 6.
The following truth table shows the four basic logical connectives. Logical disjunction is inclusive: p∨q is true when either or both inputs are true. Classical logical implication has exactly the same values as ¬p∨q; its only false row has p true and q false. These truth conditions are specified in forall x: Calgary, chapter 9.
Evaluate (p→q)∧p from the inside out: first the logical implication, then the outer logical conjunction. The final column also tests the logical implication expressing the modus ponens rule:
pTTFF​qTFTF​p→qTFTT​(p→q)∧pTFFF​((p→q)∧p)→qTTTT​​
(9)
At p=T,q=F, the logical implication is false, so the logical conjunction is false. The abstract syntax tree below separates the construction of the propositional formula from the values propagated through it. Both occurrences of p receive the same value from the Boolean valuation. With the opposite assignment p=F,q=T, the logical implication is true but the logical conjunction is still false because its second input p is false. Recursive evaluation and exhaustive truth tables are explained in forall x: Calgary, chapter 11.
The last column is always true: ((p→q)∧p)→q is a tautology. This expresses the logical validity of the modus ponens rule: whenever both premises p→q and p are true, q is true. It does not say the premises are true under every Boolean valuation; their logical conjunction is true only on the first row. For a short natural deduction proof outline, assume (p→q)∧p, extract both conjuncts, apply the implication elimination rule to obtain q, then discharge the assumption by the implication introduction rule. See forall x: Calgary, sections 17.3–17.5.
Three tests answer different questions: Boolean satisfiability requires at least one true row, a tautology requires every row true, and a contradiction has every row false. Thus p∨¬p is a tautology, p∧¬p is a contradiction, and p∧q is satisfiable but not a tautology: it is true only at p=q=T. See forall x: Calgary, sections 12.1–12.4.
Propositional logic is useful because an inference pattern can be checked once and reused for many choices of propositions. Its beauty is that a finite truth table completely settles classical truth-functional questions about a fixed propositional formula. But logical validity does not verify real atomic claims. If p means “the switch is closed” and q means “the lamp is lit”, a valid use of the modus ponens rule still requires establishing its premises about the apparatus; the truth table supplies neither an observation nor a causal explanation. See forall x: Calgary, chapter 2 and chapter 10.

A propositional variable is an atomic symbol assigned a truth value by a Boolean valuation. A propositional formula is built from these symbols by logical connectives. The variables carry no quantifiers over individuals; their values may be chosen independently.

Propositional logic OurBigBook.com
From Boolean clauses containing complementary Boolean literals, derive the Boolean clause formed by removing that complementary pair and taking the remaining Boolean literals. For example, resolving p∨¬q with ¬p∨¬r gives ¬q∨¬r. Backward proof search with a positive-headed Horn clause and an all-negative query is a restricted use of this rule.

Propositional logic OurBigBook.com
An indivisible statement treated as either true or false. In a labelled transition system, an atomic proposition p holds at state s exactly when p∈L(s).

Propositional logic OurBigBook.com
A propositional formula φ semantically entails ψ when every Boolean valuation satisfying φ satisfies ψ. Equivalently, φ∧¬ψ is an unsatisfiable Boolean formula. Deciding semantic entailment is co-NP-complete: a counterexample Boolean valuation certifies failure in polynomial time, while θ↦⟨θ,p∧¬p⟩ reduces unsatisfiability to semantic entailment.

Propositional logic OurBigBook.com
In propositional logic with the usual two truth values, negating a proposition twice preserves its truth value. Thus the complement of a set taken twice, in one fixed universal set, is the original set.

Propositional logic OurBigBook.com
Every finite collection of finite propositional formulas mentions only finitely many Boolean variables. Two Boolean valuations agreeing on those variables satisfy exactly the same formulas. They therefore have the same value under any weighted formula utility representation using that collection.
This observation limits representation over infinite sets. On N, the function indicating whether the selected subset is infinite cannot be represented by a finite rule base: if F is the finite set of mentioned indices, ∅ and N∖F agree on all those indices but require values zero and one. Completeness claims for finite propositional rule bases must therefore specify a finite underlying set or restrict the functions represented.

Words: 42
Propositional logic OurBigBook.com
A contradiction is an assertion or collection of assumptions from which logical falsity follows. Deriving both a statement P and its logical negation is a standard example. A contradiction under a temporary assumption can establish that assumption's negation; classical proof by contradiction additionally uses this to establish positive conclusions.

Lindenbaum algebra

Words: 157 Articles: 1
Propositional logic OurBigBook.com
Identify classical propositional formulae when their equivalence is provable from a fixed theory. Their equivalence classes form the Lindenbaum algebra: meet and join are induced by conjunction and disjunction, complementation by negation, and the order by provable implication. Provable equivalence is preserved by each connective, so these operations are well-defined; the familiar classical propositional identities make this a Boolean algebra. A homomorphism of lattices to {0,1} preserving zero and one also preserves complements and therefore specifies a truth valuation of the atomic propositions. All axioms of the fixed theory represent one. Separating the class of an unprovable formula from one consequently gives a countervaluation, proving the completeness theorem for propositional logic.

Lindenbaum algebra OurBigBook.com
Take formulas whose free variables lie among a fixed n-tuple and identify them when their universal equivalence follows from T. Conjunction, disjunction and negation induce a Boolean algebra; its order is implication modulo T. Complete types correspond to ultrafilters and isolated complete types to atoms. For a complete theory in a countable language, finiteness of these algebras for every finite n characterizes countable categoricity.

A propositional theory is a set of propositional formulas, sometimes identified with its deductive closure. It is a consistent set of formulae when contradiction is not derivable from it. A propositional type is a collection of propositional formulas to be jointly realized by a Boolean valuation. A valuation realizes it when every member is true and omits it when some member is false. For propositional omission arguments, the collection need not itself be consistent.

If a consistent propositional theory locally omits every member of a countable family of propositional types, it has a Boolean valuation omitting them all. One may also impose any finite condition consistent with the theory. Successively extend the condition by a negated member of the next type; local omission preserves consistency. The propositional compactness theorem then supplies the valuation. Countability of the ambient language and decidability of consistency are not needed for this argument.

Relative to a consistent propositional theory T, a nonprincipal propositional type has no formula consistent with T that implies every member modulo T. Equivalently, for each finite condition θ consistent with T, some member σ leaves T∪{θ,¬σ} consistent. This is the local omission condition for the extended omitting types theorem for propositional logic.

A propositional formula is built from atomic propositions using logical connectives. Unlike a first-order formula, it has no quantifiers over individuals. A Boolean valuation interprets its atoms as truth values and evaluates its connectives recursively.

For an atomic variable the only subformula is itself; for ¬A, add ¬A to the subformulas of A; for a binary connective, add the combined formula to the union of the two operands' subformulas. The set of distinct subformulas can have smaller cardinality than the number of occurrences in the abstract syntax tree when the same expression appears more than once.

Induct on the context surrounding the occurrence: at the root the result is the replacement formula; under a connective apply the induction hypothesis to the affected child and rebuild the parent using its formation rule.

Subformula replacement theorem OurBigBook.com
Replacing a designated subformula by a logically equivalent formula preserves logical equivalence of the surrounding propositional formulas. For any Boolean valuation the two expressions at the replaced node have the same truth value. Each logical connective preserves this agreement when its other inputs are unchanged. Induction from that node to the root proves agreement of the whole formulas under every valuation.

Every propositional formula generated by a parenthesized grammar has equally many opening and closing parentheses. By structural induction, atomic formulas begin with equal zero counts; negation preserves them; and a parenthesized binary logical connective adds its two subformula counts and one parenthesis of each kind. An optional paired-parenthesis construction also adds one to both counts. This necessary syntactic invariant is useful for checking generated expressions, though equal counts alone do not guarantee correctly nested syntax.

A propositional substitution maps each atomic propositional variable to a propositional formula and extends recursively through every logical connective. Replacements are simultaneous: a variable appearing inside a replacement formula is not replaced again in the same substitution step. Since propositional logic has no variable-binding quantifiers, this operation has no variable-capture problem.

Assume H=(P→Q)→P and temporarily assume ¬P. A further assumption P yields a contradiction and hence Q by the logical falsity elimination rule; discharge it to obtain P→Q. This is a derivation from the primitive classical natural deduction rules. The principle is named for Charles Sanders Peirce.

A Boolean valuation v assigns each primitive proposition a value in {F,T}, equivalently {0,1}, and extends recursively to every propositional formula using the classical logical connectives. The same primitive proposition always receives the same value within one Boolean valuation. For compound propositional formulas A and B,
v(¬A)=Tv(A∧B)=Tv(A∨B)=Tv(A→B)=F​⟺v(A)=F,⟺v(A)=T and v(B)=T,⟺v(A)=T or v(B)=T,⟺v(A)=T and v(B)=F.​
(11)
Every other case receives the opposite value. Thus v(p)=T,v(q)=F gives v((p→q)∧p)=F. A truth table varies the assignment; recursive evaluation computes one row. The truth-functional restriction means that changing what the primitive propositions describe, while retaining their values, cannot change the value of the compound propositional formula. See forall x: Calgary, chapter 9 and section 10.1.

Words: 147
Boolean valuation OurBigBook.com
A truth table lists a propositional formula's value for every Boolean valuation of its distinct primitive propositions. With k primitive propositions, there are 2k rows: each independently receives T or F. Evaluate compound columns from their subexpressions using the classical rules for logical connectives. This is exhaustive checking, so a formula true on every row is valid in classical propositional logic.
For a computed example over the natural numbers, let A(n) mean that n is an even number and B(n) mean n>2. The choices n=4,2,3,1 realize respectively (A,B)=(T,T),(T,F),(F,T),(F,F): all four possible inputs.
The logical implication A→B and its contrapositive agree on every row; the converse implication B→A differs on two rows. A truth table therefore checks equivalence or supplies a counterexample. Classical truth conditions are given in forall x: Calgary, section 31.2. These two-valued truth tables do not characterize validity in Intuitionistic propositional logic.

Propositional logic OurBigBook.com
A proposition is a statement to which a logical truth value can be assigned.

Proposition OurBigBook.com
A logical connective forms a compound proposition from component propositions; logical truth and logical falsity are the zero-input cases. Logical negation has one input, while logical conjunction, logical disjunction, and logical implication each have two. In classical propositional logic, these logical connectives are truth-functional: their output value is determined by their input values, as listed in a truth table. This does not characterize every kind of logical connective in every logic. See forall x: Calgary, section 10.1.

Logical connective OurBigBook.com
A binary logical connective true exactly when its two arguments have the same truth value. It is logically equivalent to (P→Q)∧(Q→P), and hence to (¬P∨Q)∧(¬Q∨P). Its truth table has value one on input pairs (0,0) and (1,1), and zero on (0,1) and (1,0).

Logical connective OurBigBook.com
Logical implication forms the proposition A→B, read “if A, then B”. In classical propositional logic, it is false exactly when A is true and B is false. Equivalently, it has the same truth table as ¬A∨B, using logical negation and logical disjunction. A false hypothesis makes the logical implication true regardless of its conclusion; thus it asserts neither the hypothesis nor a causal connection.
For example, for every natural number n, divisibility by four implies that n is an even number: n=4k=2(2k). At n=8, both statements are true. At n=6, the hypothesis is false and the conclusion true; at n=3, both are false. The only forbidden case is a multiple of four that is not an even number.
In Intuitionistic propositional logic, a proof of A→B consists of a construction transforming any proof of A into a proof of B. The implication introduction rule proves B under a temporary assumption A; the modus ponens rule applies the result when A is available. The classical identification with ¬A∨B is not generally intuitionistically valid.

Exactly one Boolean valuation falsifies all these disjuncts: A1​=0 and A2​=⋯=An​=1. Of the 2n assignments, the other 2n−1 are satisfying assignments. Left-associated implication chains have a different meaning and need not have the same count.

The contrapositive of a logical implication A→B reverses the direction and applies logical negation to both sides: ¬B→¬A. Peano arithmetic OurBigBook.com
Gentzen's consistency argument associates finite arithmetic derivations with effective ordinal notations below epsilon zero. This explains why the relevant transfinite induction principle implies formal consistency statement. For a finite slow-well-ordering formulation one additionally needs the controlled-termination miniaturization theorem, rather than assuming that ordinary proof reductions have linearly growing size. An assignment in a first-order structure chooses a domain element for each variable. It determines the value of every first-order term and the truth of every first-order formula, once the interpretations of symbols are fixed. A first-order sentence has no free variables, so its truth is independent of the assignment in a first-order structure. Quantification changes the value assigned to the bound variable while retaining the other values.

Term-generated model

Words: 51
First-order structure OurBigBook.com
A term-generated model has every element denoted by a closed term of its original language. Each element is then parameter-free definable by an equation x=t. A term model of a complete Henkin theory is a syntactic construction with this property, but “term-generated” can be stated for an arbitrary structure without choosing such a construction.

Successor structure ((N,s,0))

Words: 40
First-order structure OurBigBook.com
The standard successor structure has the natural numbers as domain, the successor function s(n)=n+1, and the named element zero. Its complete first-order theory is the theory of successor. Without addition, multiplication, or order, elements outside the zero-generated component are possible in other models of the same complete theory.

Definable set (D={a:M⊨φ(a,b)})

Words: 308 Articles: 3
First-order structure OurBigBook.com
A definable set in a first-order structure M is the set of tuples satisfying one first-order formula, possibly with a specified finite tuple of parameters b from the structure. A set definable over B⊆M uses parameters from B. Parameter-free definability uses no extra named elements. The distinction matters: any singleton becomes definable if its own element is allowed as a parameter, while many singletons are not definable without parameters. Finite Boolean combinations of definable sets are definable, using logical conjunction, logical disjunction and logical negation.
Definable function (graph(f) is definable)
Words: 64
Definable set OurBigBook.com
A function f:Mn→M is a definable function if its graph of a function is a definable set. Equivalently, a first-order formula θ(x,y) defines exactly the pairs with y=f(x). Totality and uniqueness mean M⊨∀x∃!yθ(x,y). The same definition with restricted domains gives definable partial functions. A function need not be a symbol of the language to be definable; the graph can be specified through the existing relations and operations.
Parameter-free definability
Words: 167 Articles: 1
Definable set OurBigBook.com
A definable set has parameter-free definability when its defining first-order formula uses only the original first-order language, with no additional constants naming elements. Constants already present in the language are allowed. Every such set is invariant under all automorphisms of a first-order structure. For example, zero in the constant-free additive integers is defined by x+x=x, while the singleton containing one is not parameter-free definable because negation is an additive automorphism moving it. Invariance is a necessary condition in every structure, and becomes sufficient for finite sets in a countable omega-saturated model.
Automorphism invariance of parameter-free definability (σ[D]=D)
Words: 87
Parameter-free definability OurBigBook.com
Every parameter-free definable set is preserved setwise by every automorphism of a first-order structure. For atomic formulas, preservation follows from the definition of a structure automorphism. Logical connectives preserve that equivalence, and a bijection transports existential and universal witnesses in both directions. Induction on first-order formulas therefore gives M⊨φ(a) exactly when M⊨φ(σa). Applied to a defining formula, this proves the displayed equality. With parameters from B, restrict to automorphisms fixing B pointwise. An automorphism moving a proposed singleton or taking a proposed function-graph point outside the graph is consequently a direct obstruction to definability.

Domain of a first-order structure (∣M∣)

Words: 24
First-order structure OurBigBook.com
The underlying set of elements over which the quantifiers of a first-order structure range. Relation symbols are interpreted as finitary relations on this set, and function symbols as functions on it.

Structure embedding (f:M↪N)

Words: 79 Articles: 1
First-order structure OurBigBook.com
A structure embedding is an injective map respecting constants and operations and preserving and reflecting relations. Equivalently it preserves all atomic formulas and their negations. It identifies the source with a substructure of the target. An elementary embedding additionally preserves every first-order formula.
Structure isomorphism
Words: 42
Structure embedding OurBigBook.com
A structure isomorphism is a bijective structure embedding: it preserves constants and functions, and both preserves and reflects relations. Its inverse has the same properties. It therefore preserves truth of every first-order formula, by structural induction, so it preserves realization and omission of parameter-free types.

Substructure of a first-order structure (A⊆B)

Words: 212 Articles: 3
First-order structure OurBigBook.com
An L-substructure of a first-order structure A⊆B has a nonempty domain containing all named constants and closed under the functions of B, and each relation of A is the restriction of the corresponding relation of B. Consequently every quantifier-free formula with parameters in A has the same truth value in A and B. This is weaker than being an elementary substructure, which preserves all first-order formulas.
Ground-term substructure (⟨∅⟩A={tA:t closed})
Words: 47
Substructure of a first-order structure OurBigBook.com
The values of all closed terms in a first-order structure form a substructure when the first-order language has at least one constant. The constant ensures nonemptiness, and applying a function symbol to closed-term values again gives a closed-term value. Relations are restricted from the ambient first-order structure. Every universal sentence true in the ambient first-order structure remains true in this substructure.
Simple closure (M≼s​N)
Words: 103 Articles: 1
Substructure of a first-order structure OurBigBook.com
A substructure M⊆N is simply closed when each existential quantifier-free formula over M realized in N is already realized in M. A single quantified variable suffices in the definition; iterating covers finite tuples. This property is also called existential closure in this specified extension. It is weaker than being an elementary substructure.
Existential embedding (A≼1​B)
Words: 53
Simple closure OurBigBook.com
An embedding of first-order structures is existential when every existential formula with parameters from the source has the same truth value in the source and target. Forward preservation follows from being a structure embedding; reflection is the additional requirement. Applying compactness theorem to the target's diagram of a structure and the source's elementary diagram places the target inside an elementary extension of the source.

Satisfaction for a set structure (Sat(A,e,a))

Words: 93
First-order structure OurBigBook.com
The satisfaction relation says that the finite code e of a first-order formula is true in a set-sized first-order structure A at assignment a. It is defined uniformly in set theory by recursion on the finite syntax tree: evaluate atomic relations, Boolean operations and quantifiers over the given domain. A code includes only finitely many subformulas, and their truth relations are sets. This does not define a truth predicate for the ambient universe, whose domain is not a set. Finite relation closure for set-theoretic coding gives an explicit closure criterion ensuring that these truth relations are computed correctly in a transitive set.

Elementary substructure (M≺N)

Words: 359 Articles: 7
First-order structure OurBigBook.com
A substructure M⊆N is elementary when every first-order formula with parameters from M has the same truth value in M and N.
Partial elementary map
Words: 48
Elementary substructure OurBigBook.com
An injective map between subsets of structures is partial elementary when it preserves every first-order formula on tuples from its domain. This is stronger than a partial embedding, which only preserves quantifier-free formulas. In countable models, successive one-point extensions in both directions produce an elementary isomorphism by the back-and-forth method.
Tarski-Vaught test
Words: 47
Elementary substructure OurBigBook.com
A substructure M⊆N is elementary if and only if, whenever N⊨∃xφ(x,aˉ) with parameters aˉ from M, some witness b∈M satisfies N⊨φ(b,aˉ).
The witness criterion characterizes an elementary substructure, and hence preservation of all first-order formulas with parameters from the substructure.
Skolem hull (HullN(A))
Words: 242 Articles: 4
Elementary substructure OurBigBook.com
After choosing a Skolem function for each existential formula, the Skolem hull of A⊆N is the smallest subset containing A and closed under those functions. The Tarski-Vaught test makes it an elementary substructure of N, and in a countable language an infinite hull has cardinality at most ∣A∣+ℵ0​.
Skolem function (fφ​)
Words: 195 Articles: 3
Skolem hull OurBigBook.com
For each existential first-order formula ∃yφ(y,x) in a structure, a Skolem function selects a witness when one exists, with an arbitrary default when none exists. An expansion containing these functions satisfies
∀x(∃yφ(y,x)→φ(fφ​(x),x)).
(25)
A subset closed under all such functions is elementary in the original language by the Tarski-Vaught test. Simultaneously choosing these functions is performed in the ordinary classical metatheory with choice.
Skolemization
Words: 72 Articles: 1
Skolem function OurBigBook.com
Replacing an existentially quantified variable by a fresh Skolem function of the preceding universally quantified variables. A witness independent of all universal variables is represented by a fresh constant. The operation preserves satisfiability after expanding the first-order signature; it is not generally logical equivalence for arbitrary interpretations of the new symbols.
Skolem normal form
Words: 26
Skolemization OurBigBook.com
A first-order sentence consisting of a block of universal quantifiers followed by a quantifier-free formula, obtained by Skolemization in an expanded first-order signature. Its matrix can additionally be put into conjunctive normal form to obtain clausal form.
Skolem expansion
Words: 62
Skolem function OurBigBook.com
A Skolem expansion adjoins a Skolem function for every existential first-order formula. Iterating through the successively enlarged languages, and taking their union, gives a language with witness functions even for first-order formulas involving previously added functions. Starting from a language of size κ, the resulting language has size at most κ+ℵ0​. A hull closed under its functions is a Skolem hull and is elementary in the expanded structure by the Tarski-Vaught test.

Model of a first-order theory

Words: 231 Articles: 5
First-order structure OurBigBook.com
A structure M is a model of T when M⊨σ for every sentence σ∈T.
Definable element of a first-order structure
Words: 215 Articles: 4
Model of a first-order theory OurBigBook.com
An element a of a structure M is definable without parameters when some first-order formula φ(x) uniquely identifies it:
M⊨∀x(x=a↔φ(x)).
(26)
Pointwise definable model
Words: 64
Definable element of a first-order structure OurBigBook.com
Every element of a pointwise definable model is uniquely specified by a formula with no added parameters. Finite tuples are then uniquely specified by conjunctions of their defining formulas. For a complete theory these formulas isolate the tuple types, so such a model is an atomic model. The converse fails: a countable dense linear order without endpoints with a named point is atomic, while its other points are moved by structure automorphisms fixing that point.
Paris model
Words: 132 Articles: 2
Definable element of a first-order structure OurBigBook.com
A Paris model of a complete extension T of ZFC is a set model M⊨T in which every internal ordinal is a definable element of a first-order structure without parameters.
Paris models are well-founded when their complete theory has a well-founded model
Words: 70
Paris model OurBigBook.com
Let N be a well-founded model of set theory of a complete theory T⊇ZFC, and let M be a Paris model of T. If the internal ordinals of M admitted an external descending sequence α0​∋Mα1​∋M⋯, choose formulas φn​ defining them. Completeness makes M and N satisfy the same sentences, so the unique ordinals defined by the φn​ in N would form an externally descending membership sequence. This contradicts well-foundedness of N.
Paris models are rigid when their complete theory has a well-founded model
Words: 39
Paris model OurBigBook.com
Under the hypothesis of Paris models are well-founded when their complete theory has a well-founded model, a Paris model M is well-founded. Every automorphism of M is then the identity by external epsilon induction: once all members of x are fixed, extensionality gives π(x)={π(y):y∈Mx}=x. Hence M is a rigid first-order structure.

Automorphism of a first-order structure

Words: 286 Articles: 6
First-order structure OurBigBook.com
An automorphism is a bijection from a structure to itself that preserves every operation and relation in its language.
Prime-sign automorphism of the multiplicative integers (sp​(n)=(−1)vp​(n)n)
Words: 79
Automorphism of a first-order structure OurBigBook.com
For a fixed prime p, put sp​(0)=0 and sp​(n)=(−1)vp​(n)n for n=0, where vp​(n) is its P-adic valuation. Additivity of the valuation on products proves sp​(mn)=sp​(m)sp​(n). Changing sign does not change the valuation, so sp2​ is the identity. Thus this is a structure automorphism of (Z,⋅). At p=2 it fixes one and sends two to minus two, so it does not preserve the addition graph or the nonnegative integers. Automorphism invariance of parameter-free definability therefore excludes both from definability in this multiplicative language.
Automorphism group of a first-order structure (Aut(M))
Words: 17
Automorphism of a first-order structure OurBigBook.com
The automorphism group Aut(M) consists of all automorphisms of M, with composition as its group operation.
First-order axiomatization of an automorphism
Words: 33
Automorphism of a first-order structure OurBigBook.com
After adjoining a unary function symbol f, injectivity, surjectivity, preservation of each operation, and preservation in both directions of each relation form an axiom scheme whose models interpret f as an automorphism.
Faithful automorphism action
Words: 30
Automorphism of a first-order structure OurBigBook.com
A family (fg​)g∈G​ of automorphisms satisfying fg​fh​=fgh​ defines a group action. It is faithful exactly when distinct indices define distinct automorphisms, equivalently when G embeds in the automorphism group.
Rigid first-order structure
Words: 108 Articles: 1
Automorphism of a first-order structure OurBigBook.com
A first-order structure is rigid when its identity map is its only automorphism. Every finite linear order is rigid, whereas (Z,<) is nonrigid because every translation is an order automorphism.
Rigidity here means absence of nonidentity automorphisms of a first-order structure; it does not assert the mechanical rigidity of a rod-and-hinge framework.
Compactness transfer of finite nonrigidity
Words: 59
Rigid first-order structure OurBigBook.com
If a theory has arbitrarily large finite nonrigid models, expand its language by a unary function f, axiomatize that f is an automorphism, require f to move some element, and add sentences demanding at least n elements for every n. Every finite fragment has a sufficiently large finite nonrigid model, so compactness supplies an infinite nonrigid model.

Soundness theorem for first-order logic

Words: 27
First-order logic OurBigBook.com
Every sentence derivable from a first-order theory is true in every model of that theory.
This is soundness of the first-order deduction system relative to its structure semantics.

Gödel's completeness theorem

Words: 366 Articles: 8
First-order logic OurBigBook.com
For first-order logic, every sentence true in every model of a theory is derivable from that theory. Equivalently, every consistent theory has a model.

Henkin construction

Words: 342 Articles: 7
Gödel's completeness theorem OurBigBook.com
A Henkin construction enlarges a consistent first-order theory by fresh constants, decides sentences while preserving consistency, and supplies constant witnesses for existential sentences. Countably many additional dense requirements can be interleaved, as in the omitting types theorem. A complete consistent extension with witnesses has a term model.
Henkin theory
Words: 32
Henkin construction OurBigBook.com
A Henkin theory has named witnesses for its provable existential sentences. In a Henkin construction, fresh constants and the corresponding Henkin witness axioms give this witness property. Completeness or maximal consistency can be imposed in an additional extension step.
Witness constant (∃xθ(x)→θ(cθ​))
Words: 52
Henkin construction OurBigBook.com
A witness constant is a fresh constant symbol added to a first-order language so that an existential assertion has a named witness. In a Henkin construction one adds ∃xθ(x)→θ(cθ​), with cθ​ absent from the previous language. Freshness preserves consistency. Repeating the construction for the successively enlarged languages supplies the witness property used in a term model.
Term model
Words: 103 Articles: 1
Henkin construction OurBigBook.com
For a complete consistent theory with the Henkin witness property, the term model has closed terms modulo provable equality as elements. Functions are evaluated by forming terms, and atomic relations hold exactly when the corresponding atomic sentences belong to the theory. Provable equality makes these interpretations well defined.
Truth lemma for a Henkin term model
Words: 57
Term model OurBigBook.com
A sentence with closed-term parameters holds in a term model if and only if it belongs to the complete consistent theory defining that model. Prove this by structural induction: atoms are the definition, Boolean steps use completeness and consistency, and existential sentences use the Henkin witness property. Conversely any existential witness represented by a term gives the existential sentence by logical inference.
Henkin witness property
Words: 113 Articles: 2
Henkin construction OurBigBook.com
A theory in a language with constants has the Henkin witness property when every existential sentence ∃xϕ(x) belonging to it has an instance ϕ(c) belonging to it for some constant c. This property proves the existential step of the truth lemma for a Henkin term model.
Full set of first-order sentences (T⊢∃xϕ(x)⟹∃t closed, T⊢ϕ(t))
Words: 51
Henkin witness property OurBigBook.com
A full set of first-order sentences has existential witnesses among names in its own first-order language: if it proves an existential sentence, it proves some closed-term instance of the matrix. For a deductively closed set this may be stated by membership of the first-order sentences. In a function-free first-order language the witness is a constant symbol. A first-order consistent complete full first-order theory has a canonical term model.
Henkin witness axiom (∃xθ(x)→θ(cθ​))
Words: 20
Henkin witness property OurBigBook.com
A Henkin witness axiom names a witness to an existential sentence using a fresh constant symbol. Freshness is part of the consistency-preservation argument in the Henkin construction.

Compactness theorem

Words: 334 Articles: 7
First-order logic OurBigBook.com
A set of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset has a model.

Exactly one infinite equivalence class is not first-order axiomatizable

Words: 51
Compactness theorem OurBigBook.com
Suppose a first-order theory characterized equivalence relations with exactly one infinite class. Name two inequivalent points and require each named class to have at least n elements for every positive integer n. Every finite subset is satisfied with one infinite class and a sufficiently large finite class. Compactness theorem would produce a first-order model with two infinite classes, a contradiction.

Syntactic proof of first-order compactness

Words: 32
Compactness theorem OurBigBook.com
If a theory were inconsistent, a proof of contradiction would use a finite inconsistent subset. Therefore consistency of every finite subset implies consistency of the whole theory, and completeness supplies a model.

Compactness obstruction to axiomatizing finitely many maximal elements

Words: 41
Compactness theorem OurBigBook.com
If a theory claimed that a poset has only finitely many maximal elements, adjoining countably many constants required to be distinct and maximal would remain finitely satisfiable. Compactness would produce a model with infinitely many maximal elements, contradicting the claimed axiomatization.

Compactness obstruction to an exclusive disjunction of infinitude

Words: 53
Compactness theorem OurBigBook.com
Suppose a class requires exactly one of two definable sets to be infinite. Add constants witnessing arbitrarily many distinct members of both sets. Every finite fragment can keep one set infinite and make the other large but finite, whereas compactness makes both sets infinite. Therefore such an exclusive disjunction is not first-order axiomatizable.

Finite structures are not first-order axiomatizable

Words: 51
Compactness theorem OurBigBook.com
If a first-order theory had exactly the finite structures in a class containing arbitrarily large members, adjoin constants c1​,c2​,… and require them to be pairwise distinct. Every finite fragment has a sufficiently large finite model, while compactness produces an infinite model, a contradiction. In particular, finite groups are not first-order axiomatizable.

Well-orders are not first-order axiomatizable

Words: 33
Compactness theorem OurBigBook.com
If a theory axiomatized the well-orders, adjoin constants c0​,c1​,… and the sentences cn+1​<cn​. Every finite fragment has a finite well-ordered model, but compactness would produce a model with an infinite descending chain.

Finite subaxiomatization from an equivalent finite theory

Words: 55
Compactness theorem OurBigBook.com
Suppose theories S and finite T have the same models. Let τ be the conjunction of T. Since S⊨τ, compactness supplies a finite S0​⊆S with S0​⊨τ. Conversely τ⊨S, so S0​ and S have the same models. Thus an axiomatization equivalent to a finite theory contains a finite equivalent subaxiomatization.

Löwenheim-Skolem theorem

Words: 188 Articles: 3
First-order logic OurBigBook.com
The Löwenheim--Skolem theorems control the cardinalities of models of a first-order theory without changing its first-order truths.

Skolem's paradox

Words: 55
Löwenheim-Skolem theorem OurBigBook.com
A countable model of set theory can internally assert that an uncountable set exists. There is no contradiction because “there is a bijection” ranges only over functions in the model. An external enumeration of its domain need not itself be an element of that domain. Löwenheim-Skolem theorem controls external cardinality; Cantor's theorem remains valid for the sets and functions that the model contains.

Upward Lowenheim-Skolem theorem

Words: 65
Löwenheim-Skolem theorem OurBigBook.com
If an L-theory has an infinite model, then it has models of arbitrarily large cardinality. For a cardinal κ, add constants cα​ for α<κ and all inequalities cα​=cβ​. Every finite fragment is satisfiable in the given infinite model, so compactness gives a model with at least κ elements. Applying the downward theorem produces a model of exactly κ when κ≥∣L∣+ℵ0​.

Downward Lowenheim-Skolem theorem

Words: 51
Löwenheim-Skolem theorem OurBigBook.com
If A is an infinite L-structure and ∣L∣+ℵ0​≤κ≤∣A∣, then A has an elementary substructure of cardinality κ. One proof adds Skolem functions for existential formulas and closes a chosen κ-element subset under them; the closure still has size κ, and the Tarski--Vaught test makes it elementary.

Finite satisfiability problem for first-order logic

Words: 112 Articles: 2
First-order logic OurBigBook.com
The finite satisfiability problem asks whether a first-order sentence has a finite model. It is computably enumerable because finite structures and their truth relations can be searched effectively.

Trakhtenbrot's theorem

Words: 84 Articles: 1
Finite satisfiability problem for first-order logic OurBigBook.com
The finite satisfiability problem is undecidable, and the set of first-order sentences valid in every finite structure is not computably enumerable. A halting computation can be encoded as a finite ordered tableau satisfying finitely many local first-order constraints; the resulting sentence has a finite model exactly when the computation halts.
Finite validity problem for first-order logic
Words: 34
Trakhtenbrot's theorem OurBigBook.com
The finite validity problem asks whether a sentence holds in every finite structure. Its complement is computably enumerable by searching for a finite countermodel, but Trakhtenbrot theorem says that finite validity itself is not computably enumerable.

Priestley space

Words: 40
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
A Priestley space is a compact topological partially ordered set that is totally order-disconnected: if x≤y, a clopen upward-closed set contains x and omits y. A Priestley dual space is a space of this kind constructed from the prime filters of a bounded distributive lattice.

Kripke semantics

Words: 34
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
Kripke semantics interprets logical formulas at worlds related by an accessibility relation or an information order. Modal logics use accessibility to interpret modal operators; intuitionistic logics use persistent valuations and quantify over stronger worlds for implication.

Disjunction and existence properties

Words: 46
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
A theory has the disjunction property when provability of a closed disjunction implies provability of one disjunct. It has the existence property when a provable existential sentence has a witness whose substitution is provably valid. These are distinct constructive properties; disjunction property of intuitionistic propositional logic is one instance of the former.

Soundness

Words: 31
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
A proof system is sound with respect to its semantics when every derivable conclusion is true in every interpretation satisfying its premises. Both soundness theorem for propositional logic and soundness theorem for first-order logic establish this property for particular languages and semantics.

Free variables and bound variables

Words: 43
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
A variable occurrence is bound when it falls within the scope of a binding operation that binds that occurrence; otherwise it is free. Quantifiers and lambda abstractions are common binders. In first-order formulas, a free variable occurrence is outside the scope of a corresponding quantifier.

Sentence (mathematical logic)

Words: 25
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
A sentence is a closed formula, with no free variable occurrences. Its truth does not depend on a variable assignment. A first-order sentence uses a first-order formal language.

Theory (mathematical logic)

Words: 31
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
A theory is a set of sentences in a formal language, sometimes understood to be closed under deduction. A first-order theory uses a first-order language; consistency and completeness are separate properties of a theory.

Craig's theorem

Words: 31
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
Craig's theorem says that a theory with a computably enumerable axiomatization has an equivalent decidable axiomatization. The Craig trick gives a constructive proof by encoding an enumeration index in repeated conjunctions of the enumerated axiom.

Overspill

Words: 30
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
Overspill is the principle that an internal subset of a nonstandard extension containing every standard natural number must contain some nonstandard natural number. The overspill lemma is its definable-set instance in nonstandard arithmetic.

Structure (mathematical logic)

Words: 39
Mathematical logic OurBigBook.com
A structure consists of a domain together with interpretations of the symbols of a formal language. In the usual finitary setting it interprets constant, function, and relation symbols of their declared arities. A first-order structure is such an interpretation for first-order logic.
